question.en: When would you choose Flexbox over Grid, or Grid over Flexbox?
flex-wrap: wrap gives me rows and columns. Isn't that two-dimensional layout, same as Grid?

answer.en: No. Wrapped flex lines are independent: items in one line do not align with items in the next, and there is no column axis to size or place against. Grid models rows and columns together, so when alignment across both axes matters, Grid expresses the relationship and Flexbox does not.

question.en: A flex child with flex: 1 overflows its parent when it contains a long unbreakable string. Why?

answer.en: flex: 1 sets flex-basis to 0, but flex items default to min-width: auto, so the item cannot shrink below its min-content width and long content forces overflow. Fix the item with min-width: 0 (plus overflow-wrap or an overflow strategy), not the parent. This is exactly the class of bug you only catch by testing long content and narrow widths rather than trusting a screenshot (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/min-width).

question.en: What accessibility risk comes from visually reordering Flexbox or Grid items?

answer.en: CSS visual reordering does not change the underlying DOM order. Screen readers and sequential keyboard navigation can therefore encounter links or controls in source order while sighted users see a different order. That mismatch can make a task confusing or cause focus to appear to jump around the page. I treat `order` and grid placement as visual tools only. If the order is logically wrong, I fix the HTML source order and use CSS to create the desired presentation. I test by reading the page and tabbing through every interactive element at each responsive layout.

question.en: After using order to show the sidebar first, tabbing feels wrong. Can positive tabindex values fix the focus order?

answer.en: No. Fix the HTML source order and use CSS to create the presentation. Positive tabindex creates a separate order that jumps ahead of every zero-index control, is hard to maintain, and does not change screen-reader reading order, so the mismatch survives the patch.

question.en: Is order the only property with this source-order risk?

answer.en: No. Grid placement (grid-template-areas, line placement), flex-direction row-reverse and column-reverse, and any other visual reordering mechanism decouple visual order from DOM order the same way. Treat order and grid placement as visual tools only; if the logical order is wrong, the fix belongs in the HTML.

question.en: What does mobile-first responsive design mean in practice?

answer.en:
Mobile-first means starting with a usable narrow layout and adding changes when the content needs more room, rather than targeting named devices. I use flexible tracks, relative units, sensible minimum and maximum sizes, and media queries at content-driven breakpoints. The layout should remain usable between breakpoints, with no horizontal scrolling caused by fixed widths. I also include the viewport meta element so mobile browsers use the device width. Responsive testing includes zoom, keyboard navigation, long labels, and touch-sized targets—not only a few device screenshots.

```html caption="The viewport declaration lets the layout use the device viewport width."
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width" />
```

question.en: To stop iOS zooming into inputs, a teammate adds maximum-scale=1 and user-scalable=no to the viewport meta. What is wrong, and what is the actual fix?

answer.en: Blocking zoom removes a primary low-vision strategy and conflicts with the ability to resize text. The auto-zoom is triggered by focusing inputs whose font size is below the browser's threshold, 16px in iOS Safari, so the fix is font-size: 16px on inputs, textareas, and selects. Keep zoom available and test the page zoomed (https://css-tricks.com/16px-or-larger-text-prevents-ios-form-zoom).

question.en: Where does unexpected horizontal scrolling usually come from in a supposedly responsive page, and how do you find it?

answer.en: Fixed widths, oversized media, and flex or grid items that cannot shrink below their min-content size (the same min-width: auto floor). Find it by testing intermediate widths, zoom, and long localized strings rather than a few device screenshots, and fix it with relative units, min-width: 0 where items must shrink, and sensible minimum and maximum sizes.

question.en: How does CSS decide which conflicting declaration wins?
Which wins: :where(#promo, .card) a { color: navy } or .card a { color: teal }?

answer.en: Teal. :where() contributes zero specificity, so the ID and class inside it are discarded for the comparison and the whole rule counts as just the type selector a, which is (0,0,1). .card a is (0,1,1) and wins. The arguments inside :where() only widen what matches; they add no weight.

question.en: Your reset lives in @layer reset, but a later unlayered rule overrides it even though the layered selector is more specific. Why does the layer lose?

answer.en: For normal declarations from the same origin, the cascade compares cascade layers before specificity, and unlayered author styles rank above all layered author styles, so the unlayered rule wins regardless of selector weight. Express the precedence you want as layer order, or move overrides into a later layer, instead of escalating specificity. Note that !important flips this relationship for important declarations (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@layer).

question.en: Which modern CSS features improve maintainability, and what guardrails would you use?
Does CSS nesting change specificity? Is .card { & a { color: teal } } stronger than .card a?

answer.en: No. Nesting is syntactic sugar: the browser generates the equivalent descendant selector .card a, with identical specificity. What nesting does change is how easily you write long, high-specificity chains without noticing, which is why you still inspect the generated selector specificity rather than trusting the indentation (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_nesting/Using_CSS_nesting).

question.en: :has() would let a form group style its title red when it contains an invalid input. How do you ship that safely?

answer.en: As progressive enhancement behind @supports selector(:has(*)): the enhanced rule applies only where supported, and the base experience must already be acceptable without it. Pair it with a documented browser-support policy and tests for focus, zoom, contrast, overflow, and reduced-motion preferences, because a newer feature is not automatically a better abstraction.

question.en: How would you choose breakpoints for a component library used in many layouts?

answer.en: I would avoid encoding a device catalog into every component. The breakpoint should represent where the component's content or interaction becomes unusable, and the base style should remain a valid narrow layout. For reusable components, container-based decisions can be more appropriate than viewport-based decisions because the same component may live in a sidebar, modal, or full-width region. I would define tokens and a support policy, use flexible Grid or Flexbox tracks before adding breakpoints, and test intermediate widths, zoom, long text, and localization. The architecture should preserve semantic source order and keep responsive changes from changing logical focus order.

question.en: Why are viewport media queries the wrong default for a shared card component?

answer.en: The same component renders in a narrow sidebar, a modal, and a full-width region at the same viewport width; its usable space is the container, not the window. Container queries let each instance respond to the space it actually has, so the component adapts to where it lives instead of to a device catalog encoded in breakpoints.

question.en: A container query switches the card to a horizontal layout at 40rem. What accessibility check does that switch trigger?

answer.en: Verify that the visual reorder does not decouple reading and focus order from DOM order, and re-test keyboard traversal and screen-reader reading at both layouts. Responsive changes must not change the logical focus order; if the horizontal layout reorders content relative to source, the fix is the same as for order and grid placement: correct the source order.
